#+title: tick
#+description: The open-source statistical learning library for point processes whose Hawkes simulation inspired ORE Studio's tick arrival process — what it is, its licence, and exactly where our design differs.
#+type: knowledge
#+level: cross
#+filetags: :knowledge:external:upstream:hawkes:point_process:
#+created: 2026-10-23
#+updated: 2026-10-23

[[https://github.com/X-DataInitiative/tick][tick]] is an open-source Python 3
library, with a C++ core, for statistical learning on time-dependent data. It
began in 2016 at the Datascience initiative of École Polytechnique, led by
Emmanuel Bacry, Stéphane Gaïffas, Martin Bompaire and Søren Vinther Poulsen.
Its core is an optimisation toolbox. Its best-known part is the simulation and
inference of [[id:D72B9899-C7EC-4F27-BE17-89AE6FC18A7A][Hawkes processes]].
Return to [[id:CF2C4F3A-9C5C-4E7A-9E16-2A3A8C1D4C11][External knowledge]] / [[id:7474935C-95D1-3034-B833-83DCD9FB3A09][Knowledge]].

* Summary

ORE Studio does not use tick, link against it or copy its source. The
[[id:F135B9AF-902F-46C5-847C-0820D8C92D28][tick arrival]] design takes ideas
from tick's Hawkes simulation and builds them again in the style of
=ores.analytics.quant=. Every source file of that implementation says so in a
comment. The ORE Studio licence applies to the files, because they contain no
tick code. This page records what the ideas are, what we do differently, and
where to read more.

* Detail

** Where it lives

- /Upstream/ — [[https://github.com/X-DataInitiative/tick][github.com/X-DataInitiative/tick]].
- /Documentation/ — [[https://x-datainitiative.github.io/tick][x-datainitiative.github.io/tick]].
- /Licence/ — BSD 3-clause, "Copyright (c) 2015-2018, the tick developers".
- /Version read/ — 0.8.0.2, commit =a40d19f868=. The read covered
  =lib/cpp/hawkes/simulation=.
- /In this repo/ — not vendored, not a dependency.

** The ideas we take

1. *A point process is simulated by thinning.* tick follows Ogata (1981): bound
   the future intensity, draw a candidate gap from the exponential law at the
   bound, and keep or discard the candidate by comparing the true intensity to
   the bound. See [[id:D72B9899-C7EC-4F27-BE17-89AE6FC18A7A][Hawkes Process]].
2. *The exponential kernel keeps one running number.* tick caches the sum of
   the kernel over past events, and decays it by $e^{-\beta\,\Delta}$ between
   events. Each event then costs constant time.
3. *The kernel is stated by a branching ratio and a decay.* tick's
   =HawkesKernelExp(intensity, decay)= is
   $\phi(x) = \text{intensity}\cdot\text{decay}\cdot e^{-\text{decay}\,x}$. So its
   =intensity= is the branching ratio $n = \alpha/\beta$, and the usual $\alpha$
   is =intensity * decay=. Our parametrisation also states the kernel by $n$ and
   $\beta$.
4. *A simulation is checked against its compensator.* tick can evaluate the
   compensator at each event, which supports the time-rescaling test in
   [[id:46CC91F8-3591-44EE-B19F-31CBC6D7AFA6][Point Process and Conditional Intensity]].

** Where ORE Studio differs

| Matter | tick | ORE Studio |
|--------+------+------------|
| Dimensions | Any number of streams, with a matrix of kernels | One stream. A feed has one tick stream, and no consumer needs cross-excitation. |
| Kernels | Exponential, sum of exponentials, power law, a user time function | Exponential. A stream of ticks clusters with one exponential kernel, and the sum of exponentials is the first extension. |
| Method | Thinning for every kernel | Direct inversion (Dassios and Zhao 2013) for the exponential kernel. It needs no rejected candidates. Thinning is the method to add for another kernel. |
| Stability | Not checked. A branching ratio of one or more runs until the caller stops it. | Checked in the shared parameter validation: the branching ratio must be below one. A cap on events in a request is a second guard. |
| Parameters | Baseline, intensity (branching ratio) and decay | Long-run rate, branching ratio and decay, which keeps the ticks-per-hour setting of a feed meaningful. |
| Time | A unitless double | Seconds, because the clock sleeps in wall time. |
| Random numbers | Its own =Rand= wrapper on =std::mt19937_64=, an =int= seed | =std::mt19937= from a 32-bit seed, as every process in the library does. A seed does not give tick's numbers. |
| Arrays and storage | Its own array library, reference-counted arrays and cereal serialisation | None. The process keeps one number. |
| Inference | Fits kernels to data by several estimators | None. Our processes generate data. |
| Language | Python 3 front end over C++ | C++ only, in a library that has no logging, database or messaging dependency. |

** Why the source says "inspired by"

The ORE Studio files contain no tick code. They share an algorithm and a
parametrisation name with tick, and copyright protects the expression of source, not an algorithm. Even so, the
courteous and honest course is to say where the ideas came from. Each file of
the implementation carries a short comment that names tick, its licence and
this page. The commit that adds the files says the same. If a later change
copies any tick source, the BSD 3-clause terms apply to the copied part, and
the file must then carry tick's notice.

** How to cite

The tick README asks that scientific work cite the library. The paper is
Bacry, Bompaire, Gaïffas and Poulsen (2017), arXiv:1707.03003. The Hawkes note
lists it under further reading.
